text: SEE PROFILE

Context. Optimal management of invasive species should determine the interval between lethal-control operations that will sustain a desired population suppression at minimum cost. This requires an understanding of the species' rate of recruitment following control. These data are difficult to acquire for vertebrate carnivores such as the red fox (Vulpes vulpes), which are not readily trapped or observed.Aims. To provide a long-term evaluation of the effects of 1080 poison baiting on the abundance and extent of movement of red foxes in a semiarid environment.Methods. We used non-invasive DNA sampling of fox hairs in semi-arid Western Australia where the population was subject to two episodes of aerially delivered sodium fluoroacetate (1080) poison baits within 12 months. Sampling took place at ~45-day intervals and individual foxes were identified by genotyping eight microsatellite DNA markers and a genderspecific marker. Open-population and spatially explicit mark-recapture models were used to estimate the density, apparent survival and movements of foxes before and following baiting.Key results. Following a severe reduction in density after baiting, fox density during the ensuing 12 months increased slowly (0.01 foxes km -2 month -1 ), such that density had only reached 22% of pre-baiting levels ~10 months after the initial baiting. Moreover, recovery was non-linear as population growth was negligible for 6 months, then exhibited a nine-fold increase 7-9 months after control, coincident with the dispersal of juveniles in autumn. Fox movements between recaptures were on average 470% greater after baiting than before, in line with expectations for low-density populations, suggesting that the probability of encountering baits during this period would be higher than before baiting.Conclusions. Baiting with 1080 poison significantly reduced the density of foxes, and the low density was sustained for more than 6 months. Foxes moved significantly further between recaptures after baiting when at low densities.Implications. Control programs in this region may be carried out at low frequency to suppress fox density to a fraction of unbaited levels. The intensity of follow-up baiting may also be adjusted downwards, to take account of an increased probability of bait encounter in more mobile foxes.

In Australia, the most significant pest of both livestock and native biodiversity is the red fox (Vulpes vulpes), which was introduced from the United Kingdom in the 1870s and is now distributed across the southern 75% of the continent (Saunders et al. 1995). The combined ecological and agricultural cost of foxes to the Australian economy was estimated to be AU $227.5 million a year (McLeod 2004). This has motivated concerted efforts to control foxes in Australia, and a wide range of lethal techniques are employed for this purpose (Baxter et al. 2008). Of these, baiting with 1080 poison (sodium fluoroacetate) is the most effective because uptake rate is high, large-scale distribution is simple, and the elusive nature of foxes makes more direct approaches, such as trapping and shooting, difficult (Thomson and Algar 2000;Thomson et al. 2000;Gentle et al. 2007). Nevertheless, control by baiting remains an expensive undertaking, and establishing the most cost-effective ways to implement control programs is an ongoing research priority (Saunders and McLeod 2007).
Mathematical models of optimal control of invasive species identify post-control recruitment from outside an area of control as a key parameter that must be estimated accurately because it determines the appropriate frequency of control (Chatterjee 1973;Hone 1999;Rushton et al. 2006). The rate of recruitment via immigration is intimately related to the movement capabilities and behaviours of pests (Levins 2006). Foxes are capable of extensive movement, and are often rapid colonisers of vacant habitats following population perturbations (Harris and Trewhella 1988;Kinnear et al. 1988;Allen and Sargeant 1993;Meek and Saunders 2000). There are numerous examples where despite control removing many foxes, indices of fox density, such as occurrences of footprints, have remained effectively constant because of apparently high immigration from outside the area of control (e.g. Harding et al. 2001;Baker and Harris 2006;Piggott et al. 2008). In other examples, however, post-control recruitment has been slower and associated with the immigration of dispersing juveniles rather than surplus adults from adjacent regions (Thomson et al. 2000). These variations in rates of recruitment are likely to reflect differences in the spatial scales of control relative to the extent of fox movements in those areas, as well as seasonal and regional differences in movement behaviour (Thomson et al. 2000;Saunders et al. 2010). Yet, the difficulty of directly monitoring changes in fox density, and the ambiguous results often derived from activity indices (Anderson 2001), has meant that few of these examples have provided clear understandings of the drivers of post-control recruitment (Thomson et al. 2000), nor provided quantitative estimates of fox-recruitment rates that could be incorporated into predictive models of optimal management. Instead, control periodicity in Australia is largely determined through trial and error, and intervals between episodes of poison baiting in Australia vary from as frequently as monthly (Greentree et al. 2000) to annually (Gentle et al. 2007).
The extent of movement also determines the probability that invasive species will encounter poison baits or other control measures, and therefore dictates the optimal baiting density (Tompkins and Ramsey 2007;Moseby et al. 2009;Saunders et al. 2010). Although there have been numerous investigations of fox movement in Australia and elsewhere (Coman 1988), and it is generally appreciated that movement is a dynamic characteristic of fox behaviour that changes in response to population density (Trewhella et al. 1988), there have been few published manipulative experiments where both density and movements have been measured (Frey and Conover 2007;Iossa et al. 2009;Moseby et al. 2009). This limits the capacity of managers to optimise control strategically according to the characteristics of focal populations, and in practice, the intensity of fox baiting in Australia ranges from 5 baits km -2 to 50 baits km -2 (Thomson et al. 2000;Algar and Burrows 2004;Saunders et al. 2010).
Non-invasive genetic techniques ('genetic tagging') have recently been employed to characterise aspects of fox populations in Australia (Piggott et al. 2008;Vine et al. 2009;Berry et al. 2012) and have been employed to great effect elsewhere for similarly elusive carnivores (Woods et al. 1999;Lucchini et al. 2002). By permitting individuals to be identified, they enable mark-recapture modelling of key population parameters such as density and survival. Few non-invasive DNA studies have examined dynamic aspects of invasive species populations, such as changes in density in response to population perturbations or changes to the spatial ecology of pests (but see Prugh et al. 2005;Marucco et al. 2009). Here, we use non-invasively collected hair samples from a red fox population subject to lethal control and apply mark-recapture modelling to generate one of the first quantitative estimates of the rate of population recovery in a fox population in Australia subject to control with 1080 poison. We also investigate changes in the extent of movement by foxes before and after control.

Details on the study site have been presented elsewhere (see Berry et al. 2012), and a brief summary is presented here. The study was carried out at Karara and Lochada pastoral stations, Western Australia (28 58 0 05 00 S, 116 40 0 51 00 E), which are adjacent reclaimed pastoral leases. The landscape is semiarid (rainfall 320 mm annually) and is dominated by mixed Acacia shrublands and sparse York gum (Eucalyptus loxophleba) woodlands. Minimal predator control had been conducted on the pastoral leases and the surrounding area before the present study and mostly by neighbouring pastoral leases in an ad hoc manner, to control wild dogs (Canis familiaris).

We employed eight transects, each containing 11 'sticky wicket' hair-snares spaced at 1-km intervals. The 'sticky wicket' trapped hair as foxes passed between three vertical sticks covered in double-sided tape to enter a monitoring plot containing scent and audio lures (Berry et al. 2012). We employed a mixture of linear and irregularly shaped transects that encompassed 90degree bends. By necessity, transects ran along dirt tracks and hair-snares were placed adjacent and running perpendicular to the tracks within the shrubland vegetation. Although the tracks were predominantly cleared of vegetation, in general, the dominant shrubland vegetation at Karara-Lochada is open enough that foxes can travel unimpeded. We, therefore, assumed that the placement of hair-snares in the vicinity of the tracks minimally biased our analysis. Furthermore, the even density of tracks throughout Karara-Lochada (Fig. 1) should mean that our analysis was representative of the study area. The present study incorporated capture information from the final two sessions reported previously (Berry et al. 2012), namely June and August 2008, here identified as Sessions 1 and 2, and extended an identical sampling regime of ~45-day intervals between sampling sessions that each consisted of four consecutive sampling days (occasions) for a further 12 months until July 2009 (six further sessions). The final sampling session in July 2009 occurred 20 days after deployment from an aircraft of 1080 poison baits at 50 baits km -2 , which was identical to the deployment implemented in August 2008 (Berry et al. 2012), and covered the entire Karara-Lochada study site and a further 5-km buffer from the property boundary. Fifty baits km -2 is the operational rate for feral-cat control (Algar and Burrows 2004). A large rainfall event followed several days after the September 2008 baiting, making it unlikely that baits remained viable for long after. In total, eight sampling sessions took place; however, samples were not obtained for three of these sessions because foxes were absent or at extremely low densities and hairs were not collected on hair-snares.
Sticky wickets were checked daily and hairs were removed from the tape with sterilised forceps, placed in a sealed paper envelope, labelled, frozen at À20 C and transported to the DNA laboratory within 2 weeks of collection. To limit any effect of time on the quality and quantity of DNA in each follicle, DNA extraction was carried out within 2 weeks of the receipt of the samples. Laboratory analyses were conducted under strict protocols and guidelines, to minimise poor-quality samples and reduce genotyping errors (see Berry et al. (2012). DNA was extracted from a maximum of 10 hairs per sample (minimum 1; mean 3.8 AE 0.2) by using the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Cat. 69504; Hilden, Germany).

Following DNA extraction, samples were genotyped with eight microsatellite DNA loci and the gender of each fox was determined with a male-specific sry product (Berry et al. 2012). Three PCR replicates of each locus were made for each sample. Results of the fragment analysis were analysed using GENEMARKER (SoftGenetics, State College, PA, USA) and all allele calling was checked by eye. The male-specific marker amplified only in the presence of male fox DNA. Therefore, to distinguish between a female and failed amplification, each sample without sry amplification was cross-referenced, with the amplification success of two microsatellite loci coamplified in the PCR multiplex (Berry et al. 2012).
Consensus genotypes were calculated according to the criterion of Frantz et al. (2003) where a homozygous genotype was accepted if the same single allele was present in all three replicates, and a heterozygous genotype was accepted if two different alleles were present in each of two or more replicates. Consensus genotypes for each sample were input into the Excel macro GENECAP (Wilberg and Dreher 2004), which identified genotypes differing by one or two alleles, generated capture histories, provided allele frequencies and probability of identity (PID) statistics (Waits et al. 2001). On the basis of PID results presented in Berry et al. (2012), samples that produced consensus genotypes at five or more loci were sufficiently informative to distinguish individuals and were used to create capture histories. Samples that did not meet the criteria were re-amplified and re-genotyped to obtain more complete genotypes (one example in each of Sessions 1 and 2). Allelic dropout (ADO) and false alleles (FA) were computed from the data with the program GIMLET (Valiere 2002). Identifying individual foxes in this manner is analogous to direct capture for the purposes of capture-recapture analysis.

section: density estimation using spatially explicit capture-recapture (secr) models
text: Spatially explicit capture-recapture (SECR) models generated in the program DENSITY were used to estimate the density of foxes within Sessions 1, 6 and 7 (Efford 2004;Efford et al. 2009). SECR uses the locations that each animal is captured to fit a model of the detection process and to provide an estimate of density that is unbiased by incomplete detection and edge effects (Efford 2004). We used the full maximum likelihood estimator (Borchers and Efford 2008) of density (D), and a halfnormal detection function incorporating g 0 (susceptibility to capture at the centre of a home range), and s (a measure of the spatial extent of susceptibility to capture). We identified our hair-snares as proximity detectors (allowing multiple withinoccasion captures per individual), and ran the analysis with a buffer of 10 000 m. Alternative buffer sizes and detection functions had a minimal effect on parameter estimates. Sixteen biologically plausible models were fitted to the capture data and their fit was evaluated with Akaike's information criterion corrected for a small sample size (AICc; Burnham and Anderson 2002). We tested models that maintained a constant density throughout the sampling period, D(.), or a change in density between sessions, D(session). Models that allowed for behavioural responses to capture (b), and individual heterogeneity (two-group mixture; h), in both g 0 and s, and all combinations of these variables, were also tested. Parameters were estimated with model averaging. Sessions 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8 were excluded from the SECR analyses because, at most, one sample was collected in any of those sessions. However, an approximate density was calculated for Sessions 2 and 5 when a single fox was captured by dividing one by the mean effective sampling area identified with SECR modelling during three pre-baiting sessions (Berry et al. 2012;293.3 km 2 ). Sex was not included in the models because of low sample sizes.

Open-population capture-recapture analysis, based on Pollock's robust design, was conducted with the program MARK (White and Burnham 1999). This analysis enabled estimation of apparent survival (s), capture probability (p), recapture probability (c), abundance ( N ) and temporary immigration (G). Four biologically plausible models were constructed that included behavioural responses to capture (probability of recapture = probability of capture) and individual heterogeneity in capture (two-group mixture). Models that incorporated change in survival and abundance between sessions were also considered, as were models that kept these parameters constant. This analysis was applied to all sessions where foxes were detected (i.e. excluding Sessions 3, 4 and 8). The support for competing models was ranked with AICc, and parameters were estimated with model averaging.

The mean distance moved by individual foxes between recaptures was calculated as the cumulative distance moved between trapping locations in order of recapture date within a session, divided by the number of recaptures. Individuals never recaptured were not included in these analyses. For this analysis, we included movement information from foxes collected under comparable experimental conditions during pre-baiting Sessions 1-3 described in Berry et al. (2012). Data were checked for homogeneity of variances with Cochran's C test. Data with heterogeneous variances were log-transformed. A Student's t-test comparing the log10 mean distance moved before and after 1080 baiting (Sessions 2-7) was conducted with the software package JMP (version 5.0; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).

section: species identification, genotyping and error rates
text:
Thirty-five hair samples were collected during Sessions 3-8. These were added to the 52 samples collected from Sessions 1 and 2 that represented 24 individual foxes (Berry et al. 2012).
Thirty-four of the 35 samples were identified as fox, and of these, 33 (97%) provided more than five locus microsatellite genotypes (6 locus n = 2, 8 locus n = 31; Table S1, available as Supplementary Material for this paper). Including the samples from Sessions 1 and 2, 60, 21 and four samples provided eight, seven and six locus genotypes, respectively (no five locus genotypes). No samples contained more than two alleles at any loci, indicating that there were no instances of mixed samples.
Comparisons of genotypes revealed no cases of one-and twoallele mismatches. The average per locus, per replicate rate of allelic dropout (ADO) was 0.016, and the average per locus, per replicate rate of false alleles (FA) was 0.014. The probability of identity (sibling) for the most variable five loci was 0.006, and for the five least variable loci was 0.012, indicating that the fivelocus criterion for accepting genotypes was acceptable. The probability of identity (unrelated) for both the most and least variable five loci was <0.001. Among samples identified as recaptures, the mean probability that any pair of samples were full siblings rather than true recaptures (PIDsib) was 0.003 (AE0.0002 s.e.) and the maximum PIDsib between any pair of samples was 0.012, with only one instance of >0.01

Five samples (15%) collected during Sessions 3-8 yielded unique genotypes, and thus represented individual foxes. Twenty-eight samples (85%) yielded genotypes that were present at least twice in the dataset and represented six different individuals. In total, 11 individual foxes (seven males and four females) were identified during Sessions 2-7. The initial pre-baiting (Session 1) sex ratio of male:female was 1 : 1.3 (n = 23) and post-baiting (Sessions 2-8) was 1.75 : 1 (n = 11).
The sex ratio pre and post-baiting was not significantly different (c 2 with Yates correction = 0.54, P = 0.46). None of the 23 foxes caught in the session before baiting was recaptured in any of the seven sessions following baiting.

Density was estimated directly for Sessions 1, 6 and 7, when multiple individual foxes were detected. All well supported models incorporated a session effect on density and the spatial extent of susceptibility to capture (s) (Table 1). The best supported model also included a behavioural response to capture (probability of capture = probability of recapture), and heterogeneity in response to capture g 0 (b + h). Models ranked 2 and 3 also included heterogeneity in s. The parameter estimates for Session 1 differ slightly from those from the same session (labelled Session 3) in Berry et al. (2012) because of differences in the models selected by AICc and the incorporation of data from different sessions.
Fox density decreased substantially following the initial 1080 baiting, from an estimate of 0.51 foxes km -2 (AE0.17 s.e.) to 0.003 foxes km -2 . Over the following 12 months (7 sessions) density remained very low and not estimatable by SECR, until Sessions 6 and 7 when it increased to a maximum of 0.11 foxes km -2 AE 0.04 s.e. just before the second episode of aerial baiting (Fig. 2), after which no foxes were detected in Session 8. The probability of capture at the centre of a home range g 0 was 0.160 (AE0.092 s.e.) and 0.007 (AE0.014 s.e.) for the 'trap happy' and 'trap shy' groups, respectively.

The best supported model incorporated change in abundance and apparent survival between sessions and assumed unequal probability of capture and recapture (Table 2). Temporary emigration was constant in these models. Model averaging indicated that there were 30.75 trappable foxes (AE6.83 s.e.) present at Karara-Lochada during Session 1 before the initial baiting and 3.23 (AE0.079 s.e.) in Session 2 immediately after baiting and also in Session 5 (Fig. 3). Ten months after baiting, the number of trappable foxes present in the study area had risen to 12.94 (AE4.09 s.e.) by Session 7. The model-averaged probability of capture was 0.20 (AE0.07 s.e.), and probability of recapture was 0.23 (AE0.04 s.e.). Apparent survival following the initial 1080 baiting (between Sessions 1 and 2) was effectively zero, and remained zero (inestimable) for ~7 months because of zero or sparse captures until the period between Sessions 6 and 7, where it rose to 0.68, which is similar to that before baiting (Berry et al. 2012), although the analysis could not resolve standard error for this estimate because of limited sample size.

section: changes in the extent of movement between recaptures
text: Foxes moved significantly further between recaptures after baiting than they did before baiting (Fig. 4; t = 3.41, d.f. = 18, Table 1. Models fitted for spatially explicit capture-recapture analysis of fox density at Karara-Lochada Station, Western Australia, during three sampling sessions, namely Session 1 (prebait), Session 6 and Session 7 (post-bait) Models are defined in terms of whether density was constant (.) or varied between sessions (session), and the effects of behaviour (b) and individual heterogeneity (h) on g 0 and s, and whether s differed between sessions (session).  P < 0.001). Individual foxes did not move between transects in the pre-baiting session, but three foxes moved between transects following baiting, with two of these foxes (both male) moving over 10 km in one day. The parameter s, which describes the spatial extent in susceptibility of capture, and thus indexes home-range size (Efford 2004), was 629.01 m (AE119.52 s.e.) in Session 1 before baiting. During Sessions 6 and 7 (when captures were sufficient to estimate s), it increased to 5174.74 m (AE1078.26 s.e.) and 2600.64 m (AE834.62 s.e.), respectively (values from the best supported model).

There is clear evidence that 1080 poison baiting can reduce the abundance of red foxes and their impacts on Australian native species (Kinnear et al. 1988). Yet, it is commonly recognised that even when control induces high mortality in fox populations, rapid re-invasion can limit its effectiveness or even nullify it altogether (Gentle et al. 2007;Piggott et al. 2008). This, together with the logistical difficulties of conducting control over appropriately large regions, has led to pessimism about the long-term cost-effectiveness of existing approaches to baiting in Australia (Saunders et al. 2010). However, not all instances of fox control are followed by immediate re-invasion. Our results mirror those of Thomson et al. (2000) in Australia, and several studies from the United Kingdom (Lloyd 1980), demonstrating both slow, and irregular re-invasion after control. Identifying the factors that dictate the pace of recruitment in fox populations and explain widely contrasting recruitment dynamics should provide opportunities to improve the effectiveness of control by better aligning it with fox ecology. Historically, the dynamics of fox populations in response to control have relied on activity indices and been difficult to monitor with confidence (Saunders et al. 1995). Recent investigations incorporating genetic tagging have significantly improved the resolution of fox-population monitoring by enabling individuals to be identified and facilitating robust mark-recapture estimation of key population parameters (Piggott et al. 2008;Berry et al. 2012). Here, this approach has permitted the first long-term quantitative account of change in the density of a fox population as it recovers from a severe population reduction induced by 1080 poison baiting. We have demonstrated a sustained reduction of fox density following control, such that the density of foxes 10 months after the initial round of baiting in August 2008 was only 21.6% of the pre-baiting estimate. This corresponds to the remarkably low rate of recruitment of ~0.01 foxes recruiting per square kilometre per month. However, the true rate was much lower for close to 7 months following the initial baiting before rapidly increasing by Session 6 in April 2009. Although we could not record the ages of foxes, it is likely that the rapid increase at this time reflected the dispersal of juvenile animals born outside the baited area in the previous year, because this pattern of annual movement by juveniles is typically observed in red foxes (Saunders et al. 1995).
Slow post-control recruitment contrasts strongly with most instances of fox control in mesic parts of Australia where reinvasion has been almost immediate (Rushton et al. 2006;Piggott et al. 2008). Paradoxically, foxes at low densities are more mobile than those at high densities (Trewhella et al. 1988), and should therefore have high capacity to invade vacant territories, especially considering the absence of physical barriers. The established relationships between fox dispersal and density (Trewhella et al. 1988) suggest that a 5-km buffer of baits outside of the study site could be readily traversed by dispersing foxes. Thomson et al. (2000) also noted that most post-control recruits in an arid zone fox population arrived during autumn and that this coincided with the typical juveniledispersal phase of foxes, but did not discuss why this differed so significantly from populations inhabiting mesic environments. However, they did recognise that the seasonality of dispersal in foxes offers opportunities to strategically focus baiting during this phase (Thomson et al. 2000).
If, as appears likely, dispersal by juvenile foxes drove the re-invasion of vacant territory at Karara-Lochada, what prevented adult foxes from exploiting this vacant habitat earlier? A plausible explanation lies in interplay between fox social behaviour and the availability of resources at Karara-Lochada. Adult foxes generally defend exclusive territories (Macdonald 1977), and at Karara-Lochada, a  significant fraction of the population show strong site fidelity and very limited movements, indicating that they are territorial adults (Berry et al. 2012). Within territories, however, foxes exhibit highly varied social structures, largely reflecting the availability of resources (Cavallini 1996). High-density populations inhabiting resource-rich environments typically retain non-reproductive 'helpers' within territories (Macdonald 1979;Zabel and Taggart 1989;Iossa et al. 2009). These individuals trade immediate reproductive opportunities for future access to parental or neighbouring territories (Macdonald 1979). In contrast, low-density populations inhabiting resource-poor environments typically exist as monogamous pairs (Storm et al. 1976). The fate of nonterritorial foxes in landscapes where monogamy is predominant is not well studied, but their survival at Karara-Lochada is low (Berry et al. 2012). The presence or absence of non-reproductive 'surplus' individuals within resource-rich and resource-poor landscapes, respectively, could significantly influence the available pool of immigrants, and explain the contrasting post-control recruitment dynamics. The frequency of non-reproductive foxes observed in high-and low-density Australian fox population is consistent with this suggestion (Marlow et al. 2000;McIlroy et al. 2001;Saunders et al. 2002). It follows that distinct mechanisms may drive recruitment in these contrasting landscapes; post-control recruitment in low-density fox populations may largely be driven by juvenile recruitment during their seasonal dispersive phase as observed here and by Thomson et al. (2000), whereas in high-density populations, it may also be driven by opportunism in 'surplus' animals. These alternative mechanisms of re-invasion require further investigation, including a better understanding of the age and social status of re-invading foxes in resourcerich environments. However, if the alternative mechanisms are supported, they imply that successful fox-control programs may require different strategies regionally in terms of timing and frequency of control, and on the basis of understanding of density, social organisation and their relationship to movement. Also requiring explanation is the failure of neighbouring reproductive territory holders to expand their territories to incorporate the vacant habitat at Karara-Lochada. Territory expansion following the demise of neighbours has been observed in foxes from the northern hemisphere (Sargeant 1972;Baker et al. 2000). A leading explanation for what motivates animals to disperse is to avoid competition for resources (Clobert et al. 2001). The failure of territory holders to expand their territories could indicate that resources are not sufficiently limited within their existing territories (see Englund 1980;Lloyd 1980;Bino et al. 2010), or the converse, that territory expansion is too costly in such a resource-poor environment. Alternatively, the 5-km-wide buffer zone surrounding the baited area may have been sufficient to absorb territory increases.
Once post-baiting recruitment did commence, we documented a pronounced increase in the extent of movement in foxes compared with those recorded before baiting. This is consistent with the expectation that foxes are more mobile at lower population densities (Trewhella et al. 1988;Baker et al. 2000), and it suggests that the absence of recruits immediately post-control was unlikely to be the result of incapacity to disperse across the buffer zone. Of the recolonising foxes in the present study, two moved particularly large distances (>10 km in one day) and three were recaptured on different transects. In contrast, inter-transect movement was never documented before baiting, and the mean distance moved between recaptures over the course of 6 months was 1178 m (Berry et al. 2012).
This increased mobility of recolonising foxes implies that the optimal intensity of follow-up baiting may be less than the initial intensity because the likelihood of foxes encountering poison baits should increase. According to the bait-detection relationship described by Moseby and Read (2006), follow-up baiting programs could reduce the density of baits by close to 80% without reducing their effectiveness. However, this assumes that the foraging behaviour of re-invading foxes is equivalent to foxes in non-controlled landscapes (see Arthur et al. 2002), and this has not been investigated.

The resilience of fox populations to control operations depends in part on their capacity to recruit from outside controlled sites. Foxes at Karara-Lochada exhibited a much slower rate of post-control re-invasion than has been observed in almost all accounts of fox control from Australia. The explanations for this anomaly are unclear, but we hypothesise that it reflects an absence of non-reproductive 'helper' foxes in this resource-poor region. Fox populations in these environments may be effectively recruit-limited for long periods. Assuming our findings are general for arid-zone fox populations rather than a site-specific anomaly, they have several implications for the effectiveness of poison baiting at the Karara-Lochada site and elsewhere. First, follow-up baiting in this region could be conducted at low frequency and still maintain low fox densities. Second, in regions where fox densities are low and dominated by monogamous pairs, strategically baiting during the dispersal phase of juvenile foxes may be as effective as baiting more frequently throughout the year. Finally, follow-up baiting may be conducted at lower intensities to account for the increased probability of bait encounter in more mobile re-invading foxes. The generality of the results presented here should be tested with additional studies of arid-zone fox populations.

HIGH TURNOVER RATE REVEALED BY NON-INVASIVE GENETIC ANALYSES IN AN EXPANDING EASTERN IMPERIAL EAGLE POPULATION

In this study we estimated the annual turnover rates, and so indirectly the possible maximum mortality rates of female Eastern Imperial Eagles (Aquila heliaca) in an expanding population. DNA was extracted from shed feathers collected in territories where at least three consecutive years of breeding occurred. As DNA samples could not be obtained at every studied nest in each year, minimum and maximum turnover rates were estimated. The calculated rates, 27.7% (minimum) and 35.5% (maximum), are much higher than what could be expected based on studies of other raptor species. According to previous studies territory switching can occur frequently in an expanding population. However, we found evidence of it in only two of the 46 studied territories, thus we assume that despite the ongoing saturation some level of site fidelity is present in the population. Our findings suggest the high prevalence of mortality, most likely from poisoning and electrocution, but also predict a large number of floater individuals that fill up the vacant territories.

Accurate estimation of mortality rate is important for understanding the dynamics of populations (e.g. Ferrer & Calderon 1990, Kirk & Hyslop 1998), and is crucial for population viability analyses of endangered species (Wakamiya & Roy 2009). The monitoring of mortality rate is an important part of species conservation programmes as it helps to estimate the effect of potential or real threats like habitat loss, illegal hunting, trapping, poisoning or egg collecting (Donázar et al. 2002, Smart et al. 2010) as well as the efficiency of particular conservation measures (López-López et al. 2011).
As dead animals of most species are rarely found in the field, indirect methods are usually used to estimate mortality. The most important approach relies on the family of mark-recapture methods. However, monitoring the ratio of marked and unmarked animals can yield a reliable estimate only when large numbers of marked individuals are recovered (Seber 1982). When using these traditional methods, capture, handling, tagging and recapture of individuals are necessary. These procedures are sometimes not implementable if there is potential risk of exposing an animal to serious injury or for larger bodied animals. Therefore, genetic studies are used to analyse non-invasively collected samples, allowing studies on less robust or "difficult to tag" species (Taberlet et al. 1997, Sloane et al. 2000, Horváth et al. 2005). This approach is especially important for endangered birds, the number of studies based on or applying genetic data from DNA extracted from shed feathers has increased in the last decade (e.g. Bourke et al. 2006, Martínkovà & Searle 2006, Seki 2006, Rudnick et al. 2007, Banhos et al. 2008, Guerrini & Barbanera 2009, Alcaide et al. 2010, Jacob et al. 2010, Väli et al. 2010, Miller et al. 2011). Nevertheless, only a few studies have estimated mortality rates by DNA profiles (Kohn et al. 1999, Rudnick et al. 2008), most likely because the ratio of re-identified individuals is often too low.
As the rapid degradation of shed feathers in the field can hamper reliable analysis and reduce sample size (Taberlet et al. 1999) methodological improvements were made in DNA extraction (Horváth et al. 2005, Bayard De Volo et al. 2008, Hogan et al. 2008, Beja-Pereira et al. 2009) to make such studies more feasible. However, this kind of sampling is typically used for larger species, such as grouse, cranes, bustards and raptors (Idaghdour et al. 2003, Duriez et al. 2007, Hailer et al. 2007, Martinez-Cruz et al. 2007, Bao et al. 2009).
The Eastern Imperial Eagle (Aquila heliaca) is a globally threatened large raptor species distributed along the forest steppe zone of Eurasia (BirdLife International 2009). Its sister species, the Spanish Imperial Eagle (Aquila adalberti) is localised and sedentary in the Iberian peninsula, and it is one of the rarest, but most well studied raptor species in the world (e.g. Ferrer 2001, Gonzalez & Margalida 2008). Based on field observations, mortality rate of breeding Spanish Imperial Eagles was estimated at 4.8-7.4% in one particular population (Ferrer & Calderon 1990) and 1.4-8.2% when most of the species' range was covered (Ortega et al. 2009). The only study estimating the turnover rate of Eastern Imperial Eagles, reported a much higher annual loss from the population (16%) based on non-invasive genetic sampling of a migratory and long-term stable population in Kazakhstan (Rudnick et al. 2005). This remarkable difference in estimated mortality between these populations of the two sister species may be explained by the differences in their migration habits (sedentary vs long-distance migrant), risk factors, in additions to the difference in reliability and accuracy of the analyitical methods used (molecular identification vs. field observations).
The relative frequency of different mortality causes is quite well-known in some Imperial Eagle populations based on the analyses of accidentally  et al. 2007et al. , Horváth et al. 2011)). It is revealed that poisoning and electrocution are the two main mortality factors in most of the species range (e.g. representing 26% and 21% respectively of recorded mortality in Hungary), although their possible effect on the population cannot be estimated unless the overall mortality rate is known. In this study we estimated the annual turnover and so indirectly the possible maximum mortality rate of breeding Eastern Imperial Eagles in an expanding Central European population with the use of non-invasive genetic techniques in order to enable future studies to estimate the effect of human-induced mortality factors and conservation measures on the population.

The 21,600 km 2 study area covers the north-eastern part of the Hungarian Plain and nearby the mountains of Mátra, Bükk, and Zemplén (46°35'-48°30'N 19°35'-21°50'E), a region holding more than 90% of the Hungarian, and more than 60% of the EU population of Imperial Eagles. The lowland plain habitats (90-120 m a.s.l.) are mainly intensive agricultural fields with small pastures and groups of poplar (Populus spp.) and black locust trees (Robinia pseudoacacia). The mountain habitats (200-700 m a.s.l.) are mainly forested by native oak (Quercus petrea, Q. cerris) and beech (Fagus sylvatica) or by introduced pine trees (Pinus silvestris, P. nigra, Larix decidua).

Altogether 3771 shed feathers of adult breeding eagles were collected under nests and roost sites in Eastern Hungary between 1997 and 2006 (Fig. 1). Most nests and nearby roosting trees were visited twice per year, first in June, when nestlings were ringed as part of the population monitoring protocol (Horváth et al. 2011) and between July and September after fledging, in order to reduce disturbance. As at this time chicks' flight feathers are only growing and the breeding pair is extremely territorial all feathers can be assumed to belong to the resident pair. Also it is unlikely that feathers from the year before sampling could remain in a condition good enough to be suitable for DNA analyses (Vili et al. 2013).
For DNA extraction we used feathers with minor or no sign of degradation (Hogan et al. 2008), most probably shed less than 1-3 weeks prior to the collection. Feathers were stored in a dry, cool and dark place to minimize further degradation of the DNA. The superior umbilicus part of the feather shaft was separated as described by Horváth et al. (2005).
Altogether 46 territories, where at least three years of consecutive breeding was observed were selected. As we found strong bias toward females in a previous study of Imperial Eagles where all available feathers were submitted to molecular sexing (Vili et al. 2009b) we primarily searched for the most suitable female samples. Because of this, one to three of best quality feathers of a given territory in a given year were selected for DNA extraction and molecular sexing. DNA was extracted according to the standard salting out method as described by Gemmell and Akiyama (1996). To facilitate the digestion process by reducing disulphide bonds in the keratin tissue, 10 μl 1M Dithiothreitol (DTT) was added to each sample (Weigmann 1968). The efficiency of the purification procedure and the degradation of DNA were checked before further analyses by agarose gel electrophoresis (3μl on 0.8% gel).

Each individual feather was sexed by amplifying introns of the sex chromosomelinked CHD1 gene, using the primers (2550F and 2718R) and PCR conditions published by Fridolfsson and Ellegren (1999). In Imperial Eagles, these primers amplify a larger sequence (CHD1Z, 700bp) in both sexes and a smaller one (CHD1W, 450bp) in females only (Horváth et al. 2005, Vili et al. 2009a). To identify the sex of the sampled specimen 5μl of the PCR product was visualized by ethidium-bromide on 2.5% agarose gel.

Sequences of nine dinucleotide repeats (Martinez-Cruz et al. 2002) and eight tetranucleotide repeats (Busch et al. 2005) have been published for Spanish and Eastern Imperial Eagles. To identify individual DNA-profiles of breeding eagles, two dinucleotide (Aa02 and Aa39) and six tetranucleotide loci (IEAAAG04, IEAAAG12, IEAAAG11, IEAAAG15, IEAAAG09 and IEAAAG14) were selected and amplified with the use of fluorescently labelled primers. A modified version of the PCR protocol described by Martinez-Cruz et al. (2002) was used in the amplification procedure in which a touchdown PCR was performed in all loci. For loci Aa39, Aa02, IEAAAG09 and IEAAAG14 the annealing temperature was decreased from 66 to 50°C and for IEAAAG04, IEAAAG12, IEAAAG11 and IEAAAG15 from 60 to 50°C. The exact fragment lengths of the amplified PCR products were determined by capillary electrophoresis (ABI PRISM® 310 Genetic Analyzer, Applied Biosystems) with GeneScan 3.7 and PeakScanner 1.0 softwares (Applied Biosystems), using the ILS600 (Promega) internal lane standard. Each sample was scored three times independently and genotypes were assigned without the knowledge of the sample's origin. Allele frequencies and probability of identity (PI, the probability that two randomly chosen individuals in a population will have the same genotype at multiple loci, Waits et al. 2001) were calculated with GenAlEx 6.4 (Peakall & Smouse 2006), deviation from the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and the probability of null alleles were calculated with Micro-checker 2.2.3 (Van Oosterhout et al. 2004).

Genetic tagging allowed us to estimate the turnover rate of only females in the population. As we could not obtain DNA sample at every studied nest in each year, minimum and maximum turnover rates were estimated. According to the data from nest site ranges where suitable samples were available from each studied year, when a female was identified in any two years at a certain nest site no other female was found between those dates at the same site. Any female lost from a nest site range did not reappear later in the same range. These data suggest that when one individual was identified at least twice as a resident female (first at the start of the studied period and second after the years without samples), the same individual was using the nest site range in the missing years as well (Table 1, rows a-b).
When data was missing between different individual residents, the minimum turnover rate was estimated by assuming a single change that was actually detected by genotyping, and the maximum rate was estimated by assuming changes for every missing year in addition to the one detected (Table 1, rows c-f). Both minimum and maximum rates were determined by averaging the number of turnover events in each territory, in order to avoid Table 1. Differences between the turnover rates in mountain and lowland territories were tested with Brunner-Munzel test using the "lawstat" package (Hui et al. 2008) implemented in the R statistical computing environment (version 2.12.1; R Development Core Team 2011).

Altogether 497 selected feathers were sexed of which 450 (90.5%) derived from females and only 47 (9.5%) from males. Therefore, due to their low sample size males were excluded from the present analysis.
For the fragment analyses we selected the best quality female feather of a given breeding attempt. Out of these 166 samples 153 (92.1%) amplifications were successful, determining altogether 77 different female genotypes in 46 territories. Therefore indicating that 28.8% of all breeding attempts (530) and 51.1% of all territories (90) was successfully sampled in the study area during the 10 year period.

Two of the eight loci were assumed to contain null alleles (Aa39 and IEAAAG09). In order to avoid the genotyping bias all homozygous genotypes were excluded from the analyses on these loci. On the other six loci there was no significant difference from the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and there was no evidence for linkage disequilibrium (Table 2). The PI value of the marker set was 3.7×10 -6 . Genotyping errors were calculated as described by Rudnick et al. (2005) because of the similarity of the sampling and processing methods. The 153 analysed female feathers represented 1224 genotyped loci out of which 25 (2.04%) were missing after multiple PCRs (1.22%) or could not be clearly identified (0.82%) and hence were treated as missing data.
In the first sampled year of all the 46 territories we identified 46 different females. In the subsequent years 107 individuals were identified, out of which 74 (69.2%) were the same as in the previous year, meaning they were re-found in the territory. In 31 cases (28.9%) new residents were found and only two birds (1.9%) were detected in a different territory as before (see details below).
Out of the 31 replacement events, we had data on the age category of the new and replaced females in 20 cases based on their plumage identified in the field. In the majority (14) of these, adults were replaced by adult birds. In four cases females in immature plumage were replaced by immature ones and in only two cases were immature birds replaced by adults.

Birds were re-identified in different territories in two cases. In the first one, a breeding female was found again three years later in a nest which was assigned to another territory (Fig. 2). In the other case, according to field observation, two breeding pairs were assumed to have changed their territory boundaries several times in a three year period. This was later partly confirmed by genetic data (Fig. 3).

Turnovers were calculated in each territory then averaged to obtain the minimum and maximum average turnover rates. Minimum average yearly turnover rate of female resident eagles (replacement of a genetically tagged resident by a genetically tagged new female) was 27.7%, while maximum rate (interpreting all missing years between two different females on the same territory as replacement events) was 35.5 % (see Materials and methods and Table 1).
Turnover rate tends to be smaller in the mountain territories than in the lowlands (21.2-28.3% vs. 29.3-38.0% respectively, Table 3a and b) although the difference was not statistically significant (minimum rate: Brunner-Munzel Test Statistic = -0.8035, df = 24.409, p = 0.429; maximum rate: Brunner-Munzel Test Statistic = -0.764, df = 24.237, p = 0.452).

Dynamics of a population are determined by the relative rates of natality and mortality, immigration and emigration (Begon et al. 1990). Annual changes in the number of breeding territories and productivity of the Eastern Imperial Eagle population in Hungary have been estimated based on intensive field surveys since 1980 (Bagyura et al. 2002). The population size has been increasing since the early 1990's and maximal population size has not yet been reached (Horváth et al. 2011).
Due to sampling reasons only turnover of female eagles was determined. The large bias in sex ratio of the feathers collected under the nests was most probably caused by the different behaviour of the sexes. Females spend more time on the nests and in their immediate vicinity than males during the breeding season (Margalida et al. 2007, MH's own observations).
The population in the Carpathian Basin inhabits two different habitat types: lowland areas and mountainous areas. The latter area can be considered as traditional, because it served as refuge for the species until 1990, when the first nest in the lowland was observed. Even though turnover rates differed in the two habitat types the difference, most likely because of the relatively small sample size was statistically not significant.

According to recent studies (Horváth 2009) feeding opportunities are better in the lowlands, but there is also bigger human disturbance, which could mean more risks for the birds. However, no trend was found in breeding success according to habitat type but non-adult pairs, where at least one of the birds in a pair has non-adult plumage were significantly less successful. The changes in productivity were also explored as the expansion progressed and the newly established lowland territories had better productivity than traditional mountain territories. Unlike in the case of the Spanish Imperial Eagle (Ferrer & Donázar 1996, Ferrer & Bisson 2003) in the lowland area of the Carpathian Basin new nests are established both in the peripheral zone and in between existing territories and despite the increasing density of territories there was no change in the breeding success in the lowland area (Horváth 2009). Our data implies a much higher turnover rate among breeding females than was estimated by field methods or expected from a long-lived raptor species. Such high turnover rate significantly exceeds the estimated yearly loss of other populations of both Eastern and Spanish Imperial Eagles (Ferrer & Calderon 1990, Rudnick et al. 2005, Gonzalez et al. 2007, Ortega et al. 2009), or other large sized eagles (Real & Mañosa 1997, Whitfield et al. 2004).
The extraordinary high frequency in exchange of resident birds can be explained either by (1) the instability of territories, (2) emigration or (3) high mortality of residents.
Considering that in our study only two cases of territory swapping were found, and even though breeding pairs occasionally changed the location of the used nest they mostly stayed within the average nearest nest distance, thus we can assume the stability of territories. This is also supported by the strong mate and nesting site fidelity of the species (del Hoyo et al. 1994, Rudnick et al. 2005). Moreover, replaced females were mostly adults therefore the high turnover rate could not be explained by the inexperience of breeders. Although we cannot exclude the possibility of emigration outside of the studied population, this scenario is highly unlikely in a continuously growing, geographically isolated population. The nearest breeding populations to the Central European one are in Macedonia (500 km), Bulgaria (600 km) and Southeast Ukraine (1000 km), which distances are significantly higher than the recorded natal dispersal distances of Imperial Eagles (Ferrer 1993, Horváth & Kovács 2009).
We rather suggest that this surprisingly high turnover rate is caused by high mortality in this breeding population. In recent years the two main causes of mortality of Imperial Eagle in Hungary are electrocution and illegal poisoning (Horváth et al. 2011). While the effect of electrocution remained more or less stable during the last decades, the prevalence of poisoning incidents has increased dramatically. In the last seven years 69 carcasses of poisoned HIGH TURNOVER RATE IN EXPANDING EASTERN IMPERIAL EAGLE POPULATION Imperial Eagles were found (Horváth et al. 2011). The most commonly used poisons are withdrawn pesticides that kill so quickly that most of the bait remains intact and can attract predators and scavengers. Therefore even if eagles are not the primary targets of poisoning they are greatly affected.
Despite the unexpectedly high turnover (mortality) rates the population of our study area has been increasing meaning that missing individuals are replaced and new territories are established every year. Replacement by immigrants from genetically non surveyed populations cannot be the main process as our study area covers approximately 60% of the eagle population of Central Europe.
High natality and therefore a large number of floater individuals that are able to replace missing individuals and hence fill up the vacant territories are realistic explanations of the growth of the population (Kenward 2000). Unfortunately, as in most field surveys, we cannot estimate the size of the floater population. As we are genetically identifying most of the newly-hatched chicks in the population, we will be able to find out in the following years if they are the main source of the new breeders.
Our findings on the high turnover rate and thus on the possibly extraordinary high mortality rate of Imperial Eagles underline the needs for urgent conservation measures in order to decrease the prevalence of illegal poisoning incidents and to modify the electric power lines into a bird friendly design at the key habitats of the species. *
